item.title: Trial continues for 88-year-old accused of 11 offences relating to alleged raptor persecution in Lincolnshire
item.dc:creator: RaptorPersecutionUK
item.description: The long-running prosecution of Lincolnshire farmer William Brian Chorlton, now 88-years-old, continued at Lincoln Magistrates’ Court last week. In April 2025, Mr Chorlton, then aged 87, of Morkery Lane, Castle Bytham in Lincolnshire was summoned to court following reports that birds of prey were being poisoned in the Castle Bytham area. He faced eleven charges … Continue reading "Trial continues for 88-year-old accused of 11 offences relating to alleged raptor persecution in Lincolnshire"
item.content:encoded:
The long-running prosecution of Lincolnshire farmer William Brian Chorlton, now 88-years-old, continued at Lincoln Magistrates’ Court last week.

In April 2025, Mr Chorlton, then aged 87, of Morkery Lane, Castle Bytham in Lincolnshire was summoned to court following reports that birds of prey were being poisoned in the Castle Bytham area.

He faced eleven charges relating to the unapproved or unlawful storage of the chemical Aldicarb, possession of a poisoners kit, and possession and use of four pole traps on his Pheasant shoot (see here).

Mr Chorlton appeared at Lincolnshire Magistrates’ Court in May 2025 and pleaded not guilty to all charges and the case was set to proceed to trial in October 2025.

However, at a pre-trial hearing in September 2025, Mr Chorlton’s lawyer announced that he intended to apply for a judicial review of the District Judge’s decision not to dismiss the case (see here), which meant that the original trial date of October 2025 was postponed until the judicial review application was heard.

A further case management hearing scheduled for January 2026 was also postponed as the application for judicial review was still underway (see here).

In April 2026 Mr Chorlton’s application for judicial review was rejected by the High Court.

Another case management hearing (for the criminal prosecution case) took place in April 2026 and a new trial date was set for 8th and 9th October 2026.

The trial began last week and evidence was heard from prosecution witnesses, including evidence about the discovery of Tawny Owl DNA on a number of pole traps that Mr Chorlton claims were being used to trap squirrels.

The trial was further adjourned and will continue at Lincoln Magistrates’ Court in February 2027.

NB: As proceedings are still live, comments have been turned off.

item.title: Guest blog: What happened to the 58 Hen Harriers? The unanswered questions behind Natural England’s brood management experiment
item.dc:creator: RaptorPersecutionUK
item.description: This is a guest blog by Mike Whitehouse. WHAT HAPPENED TO THE 58 HEN HARRIERS? THE UNANSWERED QUESTIONS BEHIND NATURAL ENGLAND’S BROOD-MANAGEMENT EXPERIMENT I have followed the fortunes of Hen Harriers for many years. My concern is straightforward. I wanted my children to be able to see these magnificent birds flying over the northern uplands … Continue reading "Guest blog: What happened to the 58 Hen Harriers? The unanswered questions behind Natural England’s brood management experiment"
item.content:encoded:
This is a guest blog by Mike Whitehouse.

WHAT HAPPENED TO THE 58 HEN HARRIERS? THE UNANSWERED QUESTIONS BEHIND NATURAL ENGLAND’S BROOD-MANAGEMENT EXPERIMENT

I have followed the fortunes of Hen Harriers for many years. My concern is straightforward. I wanted my children to be able to see these magnificent birds flying over the northern uplands as a normal part of our wildlife, not as a rare and precarious privilege.

That is why I have taken a particular interest in Natural England’s Hen Harrier Brood Management Trial.

The trial has now finished. The licence period ran from 2018 to 2024, with brood management actually taking place between 2019 and 2023. Natural England published its final evaluation in July 2026.

But there remains one rather obvious question.

What happened to the birds?

58 birds were released

During the trial, 59 chicks were taken into captivity and 58 were eventually released.

Of those 58 released birds:

  • 39 were fitted with satellite tags
  • 19 were released without satellite tags

The satellite tags were intended to provide a means of monitoring survival and, where a bird died or disappeared, potentially investigating what had happened.

Indeed, Natural England explained the theory behind the trial quite clearly. If brood management reduced conflict with grouse shooting interests, this should lead to reduced persecution, improved survival and ultimately more Hen Harriers breeding in the wild.

So the fate of those released birds is rather important.

What happened to the 39 tagged birds?

The final evaluation contains the status of the satellite-tagged brood-managed birds at the end of the trial.

At the December 2024 endpoint, three were still alive and actively being tracked.

For the other 36 tagged birds, there was no current evidence of survival from the satellite tracking data.

That statement needs some careful qualification.

According to RPUK two of those 36 birds had in fact already been found dead and have been included in their running tally of 149 missing/killed Hen Harriers.

They were:

  • R2-F2-20, brood-managed in 2020
  • R3-F1-22, brood-managed in 2022

Both birds had spent the winter of 2022 at the same North Pennines roost.

This distinction matters because the deaths were not discovered after the trial. What happened after the trial was that Natural England finally published the details, on 18 December 2024, after the relevant police investigations had concluded.

Two birds found with shotgun pellets

The post-mortem examinations found three suspected lead shotgun pellets in R2-F2-20 and two suspected lead shotgun pellets in R3-F1-22.

Natural England nevertheless said that their presence suggested ongoing illegal persecution of Hen Harriers in northern England.

And what about the other 34 tagged birds?

This is where the numbers need to be handled carefully.

The 39 tagged birds comprise:

3 alive and actively tracked at the end of the trial

Plus

36 for which the tracking record provided no current evidence of survival at the December 2024 endpoint.

Two of those 36 had subsequently been recovered dead, with shotgun pellets in their bodies.

That leaves 34 tagged birds for which there is no documented evidence of subsequent survival.

Then in addition, there are also the 19 birds which were released without satellite tags.

Natural England has told me that it believes all the brood-managed birds were ringed and that the ringing records were shared with the British Trust for Ornithology.

But Natural England’s Hen Harrier Team has told me that it holds no record of the fates of the brood-managed birds that were not fitted with satellite tags. That leaves an important information gap.

A summary of the 58 birds released:

  • 3 were alive and actively satellite-tagged at the end of the trial
  • 2 were subsequently confirmed dead, both with shotgun pellets in their bodies
  • 34 tagged birds have no documented evidence of subsequent survival
  • 19 untagged birds have no fate record held by Natural England

In other words, 53 of the 58 released birds currently have no documented evidence of subsequent survival. That does not mean that 53 birds are known to have died. It does mean that, on the information currently available, there is no documented evidence establishing that they survived.

That is an important distinction.

Did brood management actually increase the Hen Harrier population?

This is perhaps the most interesting part of Natural England’s final evaluation.

The answer is not simply that 58 captive-reared birds caused the subsequent increase in Hen Harrier numbers.

Natural England itself says the number of brood-managed chicks was far too small to explain the substantial increase in nesting pairs.

The population modelling commissioned from the British Trust for Ornithology indicated that the increase was more consistent with higher survival and greater settlement and breeding by wild birds.

Natural England nevertheless concluded that the availability of brood management probably contributed to population growth, particularly through increased breeding on some grouse moors.

But there is an important qualification.

Natural England acknowledges that the effects of brood management could not be completely separated from the satellite tagging, monitoring and surveillance programme that accompanied it.

That makes the question of what actually drove the recovery more complicated than simply saying that brood management worked.

And what about persecution?

Natural England’s own conclusion is also quite clear on this point.

Illegal killing continued throughout the trial.

The final evaluation says that illegal killing remains a significant constraint on Hen Harrier recovery and that the trial did not demonstrate a widespread reduction in illegal killing.

That is particularly relevant when considering the fate of the brood-managed birds.

What did the experiment actually cost?

This is another area where the full picture is not yet available.

It said that Hen Harrier monitoring and recovery work overall had been estimated at hundreds of thousands of pounds annually, involving several directorates, but that it did not hold a detailed breakdown of their work.

Following an Environmental Information Regulations request, Natural England disclosed £83,613.50 of identifiable external expenditure associated with the work I asked about.

That included:

  • £3,291.50 for satellite-tag data extraction in 2022
  • £49,999 for the 2024 National Centre for Social Research study
  • £30,323 for the British Trust for Ornithology population modelling

Natural England also said that two of the reports were produced internally and therefore did not have separately identifiable external costs.

However, Natural England did not provide a complete internal staff-cost figure for the trial.

There are also questions about the satellite tags themselves. Six reconditioned tags were supplied in 2023 but no costs were shown* against the remaining 33 tags or for the cost of their transmissions and associated data services.

So £83,613.50 cannot be presented as the total cost of their brood-management experiment. It is just the identifiable external expenditure Natural England has so far disclosed. I have therefore asked Natural England for further clarification.

What did Natural England actually learn from this financially costly experiment that displaced these birds, raised them in captivity and released them back into a predatory environment, where the majority of them were likely to be never seen again?

The unanswered question

Natural England has now concluded that the brood-management trial contributed to an increase in Hen Harrier nesting on some grouse moors.

It also accepts that the numbers of captive-reared birds were too small to explain the overall increase in wild bird survival and that the effects of brood management cannot be completely separated from the intensive tagging and monitoring programme, and that illegal killing continued throughout the trial.

Against that background, I keep coming back to the birds themselves.

58 were released.

39 were satellite tagged.

3 were still alive and actively tracked at the end of the trial.

Two others had already been found dead, both with shotgun pellets in their bodies.

34 tagged birds have no documented evidence of subsequent survival.

19 released without satellite tags for which Natural England says it holds no fate records.

That is a remarkable amount of uncertainty surrounding the fate of birds that were deliberately taken from the wild, raised in captivity and released as part of a scientific experiment.

The obvious next step is surely to find out what can still be established.

Were any of the 19 untagged birds subsequently seen?

Were any identified through their rings?

Does the BTO hold records that Natural England does not?

And, more broadly, what happened to the birds once the experiment stopped?

I have therefore approached the relevant organisations for any additional records they may hold.

Because ultimately, whatever one’s view of brood management, these were not numbers on a spreadsheet. They were 58 individual Hen Harriers and we should be able to account for what happened to them. They represent a significant cohort of Hen Harriers in England.

Natural England itself says that illegal killing continued during the trial and remains a significant constraint on Hen Harrier recovery.

So if persecution remains a problem, should conservation policy concentrate on finding ways of making Hen Harriers more acceptable to grouse shooting interests?

Or should it concentrate much more heavily on ensuring that a protected bird is actually protected?

That is not an argument against every grouse moor manager. There are undoubtedly estates and individuals who genuinely support Hen Harrier conservation.

But the continuing disappearance of protected birds means that the question cannot simply be ignored. I started campaigning because I wanted to see Hen Harriers flying over the northern uplands as a normal part of our wildlife not as a rare and precarious privilege.

ENDS

*Ed: it’s my understanding that the Moorland Association paid for the costs of the satellite tags used during the trial. It’s also my understanding that the Moorland Association paid the brood meddling licence holder, Jemima Parry Jones of the International Centre for Birds of Prey, for the costs of the removal of HH chicks from the moors, the costs of holding them and rearing in captivity, and the costs of their subsequent release.

item.title: Defra’s Call for Evidence on gamebirds: what exactly is it asking for, and how can you help?
item.dc:creator: RaptorPersecutionUK
item.description: I hope by now that blog readers are aware of Defra’s Call for Evidence on gamebird rearing, releasing and shooting. The Call for Evidence was launched in September 2026, and closes on 1st November 2026. Its purpose is to collect evidence (rather than opinions) on the impacts of the gamebird shooting industry, to help inform … Continue reading "Defra’s Call for Evidence on gamebirds: what exactly is it asking for, and how can you help?"
item.content:encoded:
I hope by now that blog readers are aware of Defra’s Call for Evidence on gamebird rearing, releasing and shooting.

The Call for Evidence was launched in September 2026, and closes on 1st November 2026. Its purpose is to collect evidence (rather than opinions) on the impacts of the gamebird shooting industry, to help inform future Government policy.

It covers the rearing, release and shooting of ~60 million Pheasants, Red-legged Partridges and Mallards, as well as the ‘management’ associated with Red Grouse shooting, and anyone can respond.

Lots of conservation organisations will be making formal submissions, based on scientific evidence, but it’s equally important that individuals respond with their personal experiences too.

Wild Justice has published a blog that explains what the Call for Evidence is about, what sort of evidence might be useful, and why it’s important to respond.

The Pheasant-shooting season opened yesterday, a month after the Red-legged Partridge shooting season opened on 1st September and seven weeks after the Red Grouse shooting season opened on 12 August.

So this weekend, whilst the shooters are out casually and mindlessly killing and wounding thousands of sentient birds for no reason other than their own entertainment, it’d be great if you could find some time to sit down and write to Defra about your own experience, evidence or information (see the Wild Justice blog for ideas of the types of experience that will be useful).

Thank you.

item.title: New date for Raeshaw Estate’s judicial review of General Licence restriction
item.dc:creator: RaptorPersecutionUK
item.description: A new court date has been set for Raeshaw Estate’s judicial review of its latest General Licence restriction. In February this year, NatureScot imposed a three-year General Licence restriction on Raeshaw Estate, a grouse-shooting estate in the Scottish Borders believed to be under the management of ‘grouse guru’ sporting agent Mark Osborne. The General Licence … Continue reading "New date for Raeshaw Estate’s judicial review of General Licence restriction"
item.content:encoded:
A new court date has been set for Raeshaw Estate’s judicial review of its latest General Licence restriction.

In February this year, NatureScot imposed a three-year General Licence restriction on Raeshaw Estate, a grouse-shooting estate in the Scottish Borders believed to be under the management of ‘grouse guru’ sporting agent Mark Osborne.

The General Licence restriction related to the disappearance of a satellite-tagged Golden Eagle called ‘Merrick’, who Police Scotland believe was ‘shot & killed‘ as she slept in a tree on neighbouring land close to Raeshaw Estate’s boundary, in October 2023.

Raeshaw subsequently appealed the General Licence restriction decision to NatureScot but in April 2026 that appeal was lost.

Raeshaw then applied to the Court of Session in Edinburgh for a judicial review of NatureScot’s decision-making process, and permission to proceed was granted, which indicates that the court thinks that Raeshaw has an arguable case, although the details are not yet public.

A substantive hearing was set for 29 September 2026 but that has now been changed to a two-day hearing on 2nd and 3rd December 2026.

This isn’t the first time Raeshaw Estate has been subject to a General Licence restriction in relation to wildlife crime and nor is it the first time it has tried to overturn it via judicial review.

This is an unprecedented second General Licence restriction for Raeshaw Estate. It was one of the first estates to receive a General Licence restriction in 2015, based on clear police evidence that wildlife crimes had been committed although, just as with the latest General Licence restriction, there was insufficient evidence to prosecute any individual (see here).

Representatives of Raeshaw Estate applied for a judicial review of NatureScot’s 2015 decision but the Court of Session upheld NatureScot’s procedures and ruled the process was lawful (here).

Whilst under that first General Licence restriction, Raeshaw Estate applied for, and was granted, a number of ‘individual licences’ so the gamekeepers could continue to kill certain species as part of the estate’s grouse moor management plan (quite a lot of birds were lawfully killed – see here).

However, in 2017 the individual licence was revoked by NatureScot due to non-compliance issues and more suspected wildlife crime offences (see here).

As far as I’m aware, nobody has ever been prosecuted for any of the substantial number of confirmed and suspected wildlife crimes that have been reported in this area over the last 25 years (see here for a list compiled in 2017).

In relation to the current General Licence restriction imposed after the disappearance of Golden Eagle Merrick, Raeshaw Estate has stated that it considers the restriction is “wholly unjustified” and claims “The estate has zero tolerance for raptor persecution and remains fully committed to respecting wildlife, nature and the environment”.

The judicial review will not establish guilt or innocence in the relation to the disappearance and alleged shooting and killing of Golden Eagle Merrick. The purpose of the judicial review is to establish whether NatureScot followed lawful procedure in its decision-making process when imposing the latest General Licence restriction on Raeshaw Estate.

item.title: Red Kite dies after being found with gunshot injuries in Peak District National Park – Police appeal for information
item.dc:creator: RaptorPersecutionUK
item.description: Derbyshire Constabulary has issued an appeal for information (27 September 2026) following the discovery of a shot Red Kite in the Peak District National Park on or before 7th July 2026. RURAL CRIME APPEAL – RED KITE SHOT We are appealing for information following the discovery of an injured Red Kite in the Buxton and … Continue reading "Red Kite dies after being found with gunshot injuries in Peak District National Park – Police appeal for information"
item.content:encoded:
Derbyshire Constabulary has issued an appeal for information (27 September 2026) following the discovery of a shot Red Kite in the Peak District National Park on or before 7th July 2026.

RURAL CRIME APPEAL – RED KITE SHOT

We are appealing for information following the discovery of an injured Red Kite in the Buxton and Combs area.

WHEN: Before or on Tuesday 7th July

WHERE: Above Buxton and below Combs – mapping coordinates were 53.293834, -1.940895

An injured Red Kite was brought to a local veterinary practice after being found by a member of the public. When initially assessed by vets, the kite was in shock and appeared to be playing dead. There was swelling and bleeding around the injured area of its wing.

Following X-rays, it was sadly discovered that the kite had pellets embedded in its left wing, indicating that it had been shot. Despite receiving veterinary treatment, the kite sadly passed away.

X-Rays and wound photos via Derbyshire Constabulary:

WE ARE APPEALING FOR INFORMATION

We appreciate that the information available at this stage is limited, including the exact time the incident occurred. However, any information could be important.

Were you in the area around Buxton, Combs or the surrounding countryside around this time?

Did you see anything unusual or suspicious?

Did you see any vehicles or people in the area that may have been relevant?

Even if you are unsure whether the information you have is relevant, please get in touch. Something that may seem insignificant could assist with our enquiries.

If you have any information, please quote 26*431851 and report by calling 101.

ENDS

My commentary:

Given the extent of what looks like a traumatic fracture of the ulna, shown in the two X-rays, I’d say it would seem unlikely that this Red Kite would have been capable of flying a long distance from where it was shot.

Yet another raptor persecution victim, in an area where gamebird shooting is prominent and in a so-called National Park well known for crimes against birds of prey.

An important scientific paper published in the journal British Birds in 2018 demonstrated the association of land managed for driven grouse shooting in the Dark Peak with the persecution of birds of prey, notably Peregrines and Goshawks, between 1995 – 2015.

Since then, there have been many raptor (and Raven) persecution crimes in the Peak District National Park, most involving shooting or poisoning (e.g. see here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here, here).

Apart from the conviction of a gamekeeper in 2011 (which was later upheld after an appeal in 2012), I can’t recall any subsequent convictions for raptor persecution crimes committed in the Peak District National Park over the subsequent 15 years.

Not only is police enforcement failing, but long-term attempts at so-called ‘partnership-working’ was also an abject failure, with the Peak District Bird of Prey Initiative collapsing after 12 years of consistently failing to meet its targets because raptor persecution was so rampant.

The only effective measure that I’ve seen was from the National Trust, who withdrew two grouse shoot tenancies on its moorlands in the National Park after seeing evidence of suspected (here) and confirmed (here) wildlife crime.

I’ll be making this point in my submission to Defra’s Call for Evidence on gamebird shooting.

item.title: More breeding success for Hen Harriers on RSPB reserves – this time in Wales
item.dc:creator: RaptorPersecutionUK
item.description: Further to reports of this year’s Hen Harrier breeding success on RSPB-managed moorland in Bowland, Lancashire (here) and on Geltsdale, Cumbria (here), there’s now confirmation of further success on RSPB reserves in Wales. RSPB statement (23 September 2026): HEN HARRIERS CELEBRATE SUCCESSFUL BREEDING SEASON IN WALES There’s encouraging news for one of Wales’ most threatened … Continue reading "More breeding success for Hen Harriers on RSPB reserves – this time in Wales"
item.content:encoded:
Further to reports of this year’s Hen Harrier breeding success on RSPB-managed moorland in Bowland, Lancashire (here) and on Geltsdale, Cumbria (here), there’s now confirmation of further success on RSPB reserves in Wales.

RSPB statement (23 September 2026):

HEN HARRIERS CELEBRATE SUCCESSFUL BREEDING SEASON IN WALES

There’s encouraging news for one of Wales’ most threatened birds of prey, following a successful breeding season at RSPB Cymru nature reserves.

At RSPB Lake Vyrnwy, six Hen Harrier territories were established this spring, with five nests successfully fledging 17 young. A further four chicks fledged at nearby RSPB Tanrallt, bringing the total across the two sites to 21 young Hen Harriers.

Hen Harriers have specific habitat requirements, typically nesting on the ground among heather and other tall vegetation within open upland landscapes. Managing a mosaic of upland habitats can provide suitable places to nest alongside the feeding areas they need to successfully raise young.

The results at Lake Vyrnwy are particularly significant. Despite the reserve accounting for less than 1% of the potentially suitable Hen Harrier breeding habitat across Wales, more than 20% of the estimated Welsh population used the reserve during the breeding season.

There was more good news further south at RSPB Carngafallt, where three Hen Harrier chicks successfully fledged this summer. This brings the total to 19 fledged chicks at the reserve since 2022.

The breeding successes highlight just how important well-managed upland landscapes can be for Hen Harriers, providing the combination of nesting and feeding habitat these spectacular birds need.

ENDS

Natural England has not yet published the overall Hen Harrier breeding figures for England this year. Those numbers will be interesting, for a comparison between land managed for conservation and land managed for grouse shooting.

Results from the last two years have been illuminating, and simply don’t support the shooting industry’s repeated ludicrous claim that Hen Harriers do better on grouse moors than on RSPB-managed land.

item.title: Yorkshire Wildlife Trust finds its voice & calls for Government action on raptor persecution
item.dc:creator: RaptorPersecutionUK
item.description: Following North Yorkshire Police’s appeal for information about the recent discovery of a Marsh Harrier with gunshot injuries found in the Westerdale area of the North York Moors National Park, the Yorkshire Wildlife Trust (YWT) has responded with an unusually robust statement. On its Facebook page yesterday, the Yorkshire Wildlife Trust said that “It is … Continue reading "Yorkshire Wildlife Trust finds its voice & calls for Government action on raptor persecution"
item.content:encoded:
Following North Yorkshire Police’s appeal for information about the recent discovery of a Marsh Harrier with gunshot injuries found in the Westerdale area of the North York Moors National Park, the Yorkshire Wildlife Trust (YWT) has responded with an unusually robust statement.

On its Facebook page yesterday, the Yorkshire Wildlife Trust said that “It is no longer enough to condemn these actions – our communities and wildlife deserve to thrive together, and it is our collective duty to hold those responsible for destroying our wildlife to account“.

The social media post then linked to a full statement on the Yorkshire Wildlife Trust’s web site, reproduced here:

MARSH HARRIER SHOT ON NORTH YORK MOORS – OUR RESPONSE, 22 SEPTEMBER 2026

We are outraged to hear that in August, a marsh harrier was found shot at Westerdale within the North York Moors National Park.

Despite being protected by law, this poor bird had been left to suffer for days until found; sadly it couldn’t be treated and had to be euthanised to halt its suffering.

This latest case of cruelty and negligence, comes barely three months after a golden eagle was reported to have been shot 17 times in northern England and a tagged white-tailed eagle ‘went missing’ on the North York Moors, it is clear there are people in these landscapes who are careless and callous enough to harm these magnificent birds, and publicity does not stop their illegal behaviour.

North Yorkshire is nationally infamous for raptor persecution, with a report by the RSPB this year showing that one in five confirmed cases of shootings in England over the past ten years took place in our county. This is not an accolade or an achievement. We want to see anyone who has been involved in facilitating criminal actions like this to be held to account.

It is clear that the ‘self-policing’ approach of the shooting industry is failing and there is little sign of those who should be responsible taking clear visible action to stop and drive out this criminality. It is time for Government to take stronger action to prevent these wildlife crimes. 

Defra is also currently seeking evidence on the impacts of gamebird rearing, release and shooting, including wildlife crime, and we encourage anyone with relevant evidence or experience to respond to the call for evidence by 11:59pm on 1 November 2026.

Birds of prey play an important role in our ecosystems, bringing awe and wonder to the majority of Yorkshire folk lucky enough to see them, their appearance in our skies are down to the work of conservation bodies, volunteers and local people. Persecution robs everyone the chance of seeing these special birds and destroys all those years of effort.

We urge anyone who has information that can help North Yorkshire Police establish who was involved in this case to contact them. It is no longer enough to condemn these actions – our communities and wildlife deserve to thrive together, and it is our collective duty to hold those responsible for destroying our wildlife to account.

You can contact North Yorkshire Police on 101 or emailing kimberley.laws@northyorkshire.police.uk, quoting incident number 12260171320.

ENDS

With the exception of Derbyshire Wildlife Trust, it’s quite unusual to see any of the country’s Wildlife Trusts speaking out so clearly and forcefully on the issue of raptor persecution. It’s long been a bugbear of mine that organisations like the Wildlife Trusts, who are in a position of authority and influence, have shied away from prominent campaigning on this issue.

So I applaud Yorkshire Wildlife Trust for its unequivocal stance and hope that other Wildlife Trusts will follow its lead and not be too frightened by the inevitable backlash from the game-shooting industry, who are probably already composing threats to report the YWT to the Charities Commission, in the same way the Moorland Association did against the charity ‘Friends of the Dales’ for its Eyes to the Skies campaign earlier this year.

item.title: Marsh Harrier found shot in North York Moors National Park – Police appeal for information
item.dc:creator: RaptorPersecutionUK
item.description: Press release from North Yorkshire Police (21 September 2026): Marsh Harrier found shot in North York Moors On 28 August 2026 a juvenile Marsh Harrier was found in the Westerdale area suffering from injuries that left it unable to fly. Following examination, it was established that the bird had been shot and is believed to … Continue reading "Marsh Harrier found shot in North York Moors National Park – Police appeal for information"
item.content:encoded:
Press release from North Yorkshire Police (21 September 2026):

Marsh Harrier found shot in North York Moors

On 28 August 2026 a juvenile Marsh Harrier was found in the Westerdale area suffering from injuries that left it unable to fly.

Following examination, it was established that the bird had been shot and is believed to have been lying injured for several days prior to being found. Unfortunately, the injuries were so severe that there was no prospect of recovery, and on welfare grounds the bird had to be humanely euthanised.

The Marsh Harrier is a specially protected bird of prey under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981. It is an offence to intentionally kill, injure or disturb these birds, or to damage or destroy their nests or eggs.

North Yorkshire Police are appealing for information in connection with this incident. Anyone who may have witnessed suspicious activity in the area, or who has information that could assist the investigation, is asked to contact North Yorkshire Police on 101 or emailing kimberley.laws@northyorkshire.police.uk, quoting incident number 12260171320.

If you have concerns regarding the persecution of birds of prey or any other wildlife crime, please report the matter to the police. Information from the public can play a vital role in helping to protect wildlife and bring offenders to justice.

ENDS

Yet another raptor persecution victim, in a so-called National Park, in an area where gamebird shooting is prominent, and in an area well known as a wildlife crime hotspot (e.g. see here, here and here).

And not the first Marsh Harrier victim in Yorkshire either – for others see here, here and here.

In 2017/2018 Amanda Anderson (then of the Moorland Association, the grouse moor owners’ lobby group in England) denied that her members were interested in obtaining licences permitting them to kill Marsh Harriers but several witnesses said otherwise.

Motive, means, opportunity. They’re all there, in spades, but the standard of evidence required to charge someone with the alleged shooting probably is not; without a direct witness in this remote landscape, there’s the (albeit slim) possibility that it wasn’t someone connected with gamebird shooting who shot this Marsh Harrier, and that’s enough reasonable doubt for this case to never get anywhere near a court of law.

Apart from the 2008 conviction of three gamekeepers on the Snilesworth Estate, I actually can’t remember anybody being charged and prosecuted for crimes against birds of prey in the North York Moors National Park in the following 18 years, despite a high volume of recorded crimes during this period*.

The closest the police have come was probably the Bransdale case during lockdown in 2020, where a witness reported seeing a number of armed men shooting at Buzzards on an estate in the North York Moors National Park, and five dead Buzzards were later found buried under rocks – four had definitely been shot and the fifth had probably been shot. Despite extensive investigative efforts by the police, there wasn’t sufficient evidence to charge anyone (see here).

Perhaps visitors and local residents of this National Park (and all the other National Parks where raptors are still targeted by criminals within the gamebird shooting industry) will consider making a submission to Defra’s current Call for Evidence on all aspects of gamebird shooting, to share their experience of finding injured and/or dead raptors in the National Park, or their disappointment at not being able to enjoy seeing the full suite of UK birds of prey that should naturally be breeding in these so-called protected landscapes.

You don’t even have to wade through the 100+ questions on the official submissions form to provide your evidence. You can simply write about your first-hand experience in an email, addressed to Gamebirds@defra.gov.uk (write ‘Call for Evidence’ in the subject line) and it’ll be accepted in to the review.

Closing date is 1 November 2026.

*Update: Thanks to the blog reader who reminded me about the 2013 conviction of gamekeeper Shaun Allanson for offences committed on the Blansby Estate, near Pickering, right on the edge of the North York Moors National Park.

item.title: Reported Pheasant numbers in England don’t add up
item.dc:creator: RaptorPersecutionUK
item.description: Earlier this month, researcher, writer and campaigner Guy Shrubsole blogged about his latest examination of reported Pheasants numbers in England. As he’s done in previous years (e.g. see here), Guy submitted a Freedom of Information request to the Government’s Animal & Plant Health Agency (APHA) asking for the official figures on the number of Pheasants … Continue reading "Reported Pheasant numbers in England don’t add up"
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this month, researcher, writer and campaigner Guy Shrubsole blogged about his latest examination of reported Pheasants numbers in England.

As he’s done in previous years (e.g. see here), Guy submitted a Freedom of Information request to the Government’s Animal & Plant Health Agency (APHA) asking for the official figures on the number of Pheasants being bred, reared and released in England. It’s a legal requirement for keepers of captive birds, including gamebirds, to register.

As of August 2026, according to the latest FoI response, 26.37 million Pheasants were reported as being bred, reared or released in England. This compares to 25.9 million Pheasants reported in July 2025, and 25.7 million Pheasants reported in January 2024.

Guy suggests two possible explanations for the ongoing increase in reported Pheasant numbers:

a) The industry is gradually getting better at reporting; or,

b) The figures simply reflect an ongoing expansion in the size of the industry.

Whatever the explanation, these figures are still well below the estimated 50 million Pheasants that are known to be released annually into the countryside; a figure provided by the gamebird shooting industry itself, even when the source is masquerading as ‘The UK’s Conservation Factchecking Resource‘, which is actually a website run by the Game & Wildlife Conservation Trust, (GWCT).

That’s an awful lot of Pheasants (approx 24 million) still unaccounted for in the ‘official’ records.

Guy’s blog helpfully includes a link to a spreadsheet with this year’s ‘official’ figures, broken down into categories of birds being bred, reared and released in England. He also includes a summary of the data for the last three years:

These figures are very revealing, because they show a large discrepancy between the number of Pheasants being bred and reared for shooting and the number of Pheasants being released for shooting.

They don’t add up!

What happened to the 5-6 million Pheasants that were reported as being bred and reared that weren’t subsequently released?

Has anyone at APHA noticed this discrepancy? If so, what action is being taken? Is there any monitoring? Are there any compliance checks?

Failure to register with APHA is an offence, but it’s been going on for years. In a Natural England and BASC-commissioned report published in 2020, registration compliance (for Pheasant keepers) was estimated to be less than 25%.

This low level of compliance on registering Pheasants will come as no surprise to anyone who pays attention to the behaviour of the UK gamebird shooting industry. It’s not an industry celebrated for adherence to the law on many issues, including the illegal killing of birds of prey, the illegal setting and use of traps, the illegal possession, storage and use of pesticides and poisons, the illegal burning of deep peat moorland, the illegal use of toxic lead ammunition to kill waterfowl, the illegal release of gamebirds in Special Protection Areas etc etc.

Submissions to Defra’s current Call for Evidence on all aspects of the gamebird shooting industry are going to be fascinating.

item.content:encoded:
Press release from RSPB, 18 September 2026:

CAUTIOUS OPTIMISM AS RECORD YEAR FOR HEN HARRIER CHICKS AT RSPB GELTSDALE

Thirteen Hen Harrier chicks have successfully fledged at RSPB Geltsdale in Cumbria. The remarkable achievement marks the highest number of Hen Harrier chicks to fledge at the nature reserve in a single breeding season since records began more than a century ago. It reflects the dedication of reserve staff and volunteers, who worked tirelessly to protect nesting birds and support the adults as they raised their young.

The success offers hope for the species’ recovery, but illegal persecution remains a major threat for this spectacular bird of prey. Once hunted to extinction as a breeding bird in England by 1900, Hen Harriers returned to the north Pennines in the 1950s. However, the illegal killing of these amazing birds, that are celebrated for their sky dancing, has continued and to this day they still are only found at a handful of sites in England.  

Despite this year’s success, illegal persecution continues to limit the recovery of Hen Harriers in England. This year at Geltsdale, staff set up Natural England-licensed diversionary feeding stations. This well-established technique is used to minimise the adults preying on grouse on neighbouring shooting estates when they are feeding their young. Staff also actively monitored the nesting sites day and night to minimise disturbance, working around the clock.  

Celebrating the news, Ian Ryding, reserve manager at RSPB Geltsdale said: 

“Hen Harriers are amazing birds, their sky dancing as the male passes food to the female is a spectacular sight everyone visiting the Cumbria should have the chance to see. But sadly, even as we celebrate this amazing success that should be giving us hope for the future of a Red-listed species, there is the spectre that these birds will soon be targeted by those who think nothing of killing our wildlife when it threatens their profits. 

“By supporting both parents we have seen three nests thrive and 13 chicks fledge, the most for at least a century in this part of the world. We hope to see these chicks return in future years to raise their own families, but unfortunately we fear that for that to happen we will need to see more done to stop the illegal killing of these special birds“.

According to Government estimates, England’s uplands have the capacity to support at least 300 pairs of Hen Harriers. Yet the species remains on the UK Red List and far below its potential population size.  

Evidence gathered over many years continues to show that illegal persecution is one of the principal barriers to recovery, with many birds disappearing in and around areas managed for grouse shooting. The RSPB is therefore calling for the introduction of licensing for gamebird shooting across the UK.  

A licensing system, similar to that introduced for grouse moor management in Scotland in 2024, would be a proportionate and cost-effective measure aimed at deterring wildlife crime and helping to secure a future for Hen Harriers. Without further action, conservation successes such as this year’s record breeding season at RSPB Geltsdale risk remaining the exception rather than becoming the norm.  

This year’s success at RSPB Geltsdale is an amazing and much needed success for Hen Harriers, and a credit to the hard work of the people involved in helping these birds get the best possible start to life. A number of the chicks have already been tagged so their progress can be tracked as they set out into the world.  

Ian Ryding concluded: “For now, thirteen young Hen Harriers taking to the skies above Geltsdale is a reason to celebrate. The challenge is ensuring they survive long enough to return and raise families of their own“.

ENDS

Great news from the RSPB’s Geltsdale Reserve, and yet more evidence that Hen Harriers can do really well on RSPB-managed moorland (see this year’s success at Bowland this year, here), especially when they’re encouraged not to hunt on nearby grouse moors, where there’s a long history of hunting males ‘disappearing’ (e.g. at Geltsdale: 1 x hunting male in 2020, 2 x hunting males in 2021, 2 x hunting males in 2023, 2 x hunting males in 2025, see here, here, and here) or being found dead with gunshot injuries (e.g. 1 x hunting male in 2023, here).

Funnily enough, I’ve yet to see any evidence of record Hen Harrier breeding success on English grouse moors this year, despite the repeated claims by shooters on social media that ‘Hen Harriers do better on grouse moors than on RSPB-managed moors‘.

The evidence just doesn’t support that myth – e.g. see here for last year’s report from Natural England, where perhaps 3 of 39 Hen Harrier breeding attempts were on privately-owned grouse moors. Natural England has not yet published the figures for this year’s Hen Harrier breeding attempts.

I’m afraid I don’t agree with the RSPB’s call for gamebird licensing. It isn’t working in Scotland, where grouse shoot licensing was introduced in 2024 and yet the illegal killing of birds of prey continues without significant consequence, so there’s no reason to believe that licensing would work in England. Athough licensing would definitely be better than maintaining the status quo, I just don’t see it as a long-term solution.

Defra’s current Call for Evidence on all aspects of gamebird rearing, releasing and shooting in England, which will be used to inform future policy in this area, is very welcome. More on that next week.
